questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Aggregate demand curve construction
questions.learningObjective: explain why the aggregate demand curve slopes downward
questions.stem: In the expenditure model the aggregate demand curve is drawn with the price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal one. What makes the curve slope downward?

options.text: A lower price level raises the real value of money balances, cuts interest rates, and lifts planned spending, so more output is demanded at every price level
A lower price level reduces the real value of every outstanding contract, which mechanically raises the output demanded at each price level
options.misconception: reads a general fall in the price level as if it were an increase in real wealth

options.text: A lower price level makes domestic goods cheaper than foreign ones, so exports rise and imports fall at every price level
options.misconception: credits the whole slope to net exports and forgets the interest rate channel

options.text: A lower price level cuts the real wage, which pulls more labour into the economy and so lifts output demanded at every price level
options.misconception: reverses the real wage effect, since a lower price level lowers rather than raises the real wage

questions.explanation: With the price level on the vertical axis, a rise in real balances M/P is a rise in the quantity of money available to hold at any given money demand schedule, so interest rates fall and planned investment rises. The three linked effects are the real balance effect, the interest rate effect, and the exchange rate effect, and all three act through spending. A fall in the price level does raise the real value of deposits, but that is a general fall in the price level, not a change in the real value of the money stock, and it is not what the aggregate demand curve measures. The exchange rate effect does not by itself generate the slope either, because it works by way of the same interest rate channel rather than independently.
questions.hint: Ask which spending decisions respond to a fall in the price level when the money stock is fixed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Real balance, interest rate and exchange rate effects
questions.learningObjective: identify the linked channels through which a lower price level raises spending
questions.stem: With the money stock and policy fixed, a fall in the price level raises aggregate demand through a chain of linked steps. Which of the following belong to that chain? Select all that apply.

options.text: Real money balances rise, which lowers interest rates and raises planned investment spending
Domestic prices fall relative to foreign prices, so net exports rise and planned expenditure on the product rises
The opportunity cost of holding money falls, so the quantity of money households and firms choose to hold declines
National saving rises across the economy, which finances a larger volume of domestic investment spending
options.misconception: assumes a fall in the price level mechanically raises national saving

questions.explanation: A fall in the price level with a fixed money stock raises M/P, which loosens the money market and lowers interest rates, which raises investment, which raises net exports because domestic goods become cheaper. The same rise in M/P also lowers the opportunity cost of holding money rather than bonds, so the chosen money holdings fall and the spending that funds them rises. National saving is a decision about out-of-pocket spending against income, and nothing in a change of the price level forces households to save more, so the saving step is not part of the chain.
questions.hint: Follow what a fixed money stock does to real balances, then to rates, then to spending.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Shifts versus movements along aggregate demand
questions.learningObjective: correct the belief that a change in the price level shifts the aggregate demand curve
questions.stem: A student writes that a fall in the general price level shifts the aggregate demand curve down and to the left, because the curve is drawn on a graph whose vertical axis is the price level. What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: The price level is the variable on the vertical axis, so a change in it produces a movement along a given curve rather than a shift of that curve
Aggregate demand shifts down and to the left whenever the price level falls, so the student's description of the direction is correct
options.misconception: accepts a change in the vertical-axis variable as a shift of the curve

options.text: The curve shifts rather than moves only when the nominal money stock is changed by the central bank
options.misconception: restricts the source of shifts to monetary policy and ignores every other shifter

options.text: Aggregate demand never responds to the price level, so the student's claim fails for a different reason altogether
options.misconception: denies the price level any effect on spending and rejects the model

questions.explanation: A curve is shifted by a change in a determinant other than the variable plotted on an axis, so with the price level on the vertical axis a change in the price level traces out points on one curve. What shifts aggregate demand is a change in the money stock, the price of a factor abroad, foreign income, domestic wealth, fiscal policy, or confidence. Confusing the vertical-axis variable with a shifter is the same error that makes a demand curve look as if it moves when its own variable changes, and it destroys the distinction the model is built on.
questions.hint: Ask whether the price level is a shifter or the variable the curve is drawn against.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Slope of aggregate demand from the spending schedule
questions.learningObjective: derive the slope of the aggregate demand curve from the aggregate expenditure line
questions.stem: Planned spending in an economy is written as the aggregate expenditure line AE = A + 0.8Y + 0.5P, where the positive coefficient on the price level captures the real balance and interest rate effects. What is the slope of the aggregate demand curve, defined as change in the price level per unit change in real output?

options.text: 0.4, because 0.2Y = A + 0.5P rearranges to a change in the price level of 0.4 per unit of output
0.5, because the coefficient on the price level in the spending line is the slope of the demand curve
options.misconception: uses the spending-line coefficient on the price level as the slope of the curve

options.text: 2.5, because 0.2Y = A + 0.5P rearranges to 2.5 units of output per unit of the price level
options.misconception: reports the reciprocal slope and forgets which variable is on the vertical axis

options.text: 1.25, because the inverse of 0.8 is the multiplier that carries the slope of the curve
options.misconception: divides by the marginal propensity to consume and reports a number with no derivation

questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires Y = AE, so Y = A + 0.8Y + 0.5P, which gives 0.2Y = A + 0.5P and therefore P = 0.4Y minus 2A. The slope with the price level on the vertical axis is therefore 0.4, and the alternative route confirms it: the spending line implies that 1 unit of the price level supports 2.5 units of output, so the inverse, 1 over 2.5, is 0.4. A flatter aggregate demand curve, that is a smaller slope, comes from a higher marginal propensity to consume or a stronger price level response of spending, since either raises the number 1 minus c relative to 0.5.
questions.hint: Set spending equal to output, then solve for the price level.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Real value of the money stock
questions.learningObjective: compute the change in real money balances produced by a change in the price level
questions.stem: The nominal money stock is 1,000 billion and the price level index falls from 100 to 90. Holding the money stock fixed, by what percentage does the real value of the money stock rise?

options.text: 11.1 percent, because 1,000 over 90 divided by 1,000 over 100 is 100 over 90 minus one
10.0 percent, because the price level index fell by exactly ten points out of one hundred
options.misconception: reads the fall in the price index as the rise in real balances

options.text: minus 10.0 percent, because a lower price level destroys part of the nominal money stock
options.misconception: treats a change in the deflator as if it reduced the quantity of money

options.text: 90.0 percent, because 90 divided by 100 leaves nine tenths of the real stock behind
options.misconception: divides the two index values instead of forming the ratio of balances

questions.explanation: Real balances are the nominal stock divided by the price level, so they rise from 1,000 over 100, that is 10, to 1,000 over 90, that is 11.111, and the change is 11.111 over 10 minus one, or 11.1 percent. The check that matters is the direction of the ratio: with the numerator fixed, a smaller divisor gives a larger quotient, so real balances rise. That loosening is what lowers interest rates and supports spending, and it is also why a fall in the price level is expansionary in the short run but not in the long run.
questions.hint: Divide the nominal stock by each price index before comparing.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Aggregate demand in the extreme case
questions.learningObjective: state the limiting case in which the aggregate demand curve is vertical
questions.stem: Suppose every household in an economy sets consumption equal to a fixed share of its income with a marginal propensity to consume of zero, and no interest rate responds to the price level. What shape does the aggregate demand curve take?

options.text: Vertical at a fixed level of output, because no channel from the price level to spending survives in that economy
Horizontal, because with no consumption response the price level cannot affect the volume of spending at all
options.misconception: draws a horizontal curve, which would require spending to be completely unresponsive to output

options.text: Upward sloping, because a lower price level raises real balances and thereby increases investment spending
options.misconception: gives the price level a positive effect on spending, which is the wrong sign

options.text: Flat at the bottom of the diagram, because a zero marginal propensity to consume destroys the whole expenditure multiplier
options.misconception: confuses a zero marginal propensity to consume with a zero response of the price level

questions.explanation: The slope of the aggregate demand curve is the ratio of the marginal propensity to spend out of income to the strength of the price level's effect on spending, so a marginal propensity to consume of zero with no interest rate response drives that ratio to infinity and the curve becomes vertical. A horizontal curve is the other limit, where spending ignores both income and the price level, which is not what a zero marginal propensity to consume describes. The vertical case is the classical one, in which money is neutral and only the price level moves, and it is worth recognising because it is the assumption the classical dichotomy makes rather than something the data deliver.
questions.hint: Look at the ratio of the income response of spending to the price level response.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Capital deepening and potential output
questions.learningObjective: compute the effect of a change in the capital stock on potential output
questions.stem: An economy's production function is Y = K^0.3 L^0.7. With the capital stock at 1,000 and employment at 1,000, output is 1,000 billion. If the capital stock alone rises by 10 percent and employment is unchanged, by what percent does potential output rise? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A 10 percent rise in the capital stock enters the production function to the power 0.3, so the exact multiplier is 1.1 raised to 0.3, which is 1.029006, and output rises 2.9006 percent. The second route is the constant-returns shortcut, which weights the input change by its exponent and gives 0.3 times 10, that is 3 percent, a good approximation to the exact 2.9. The gap between the two is the second-order term, and it is the reason a 10 percent change in one input cannot be handled as if the function were linear in all inputs at once.
questions.hint: Raise the growth factor to the power of the input's exponent.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Determinants of potential output
questions.learningObjective: select the changes that shift the long-run aggregate supply curve
questions.stem: The long-run aggregate supply curve is vertical at the economy's potential output. Which of the following shifts that vertical line? Select all that apply.

options.text: A sustained rise in the accumulated capital stock, which raises the output the existing workforce can produce
A permanent increase in the working-age population, which raises the labour input to production
A lasting improvement in total factor productivity, which raises output from unchanged inputs
A one-year rise in the general price level, which raises the money value of the same physical output
options.misconception: treats a change in the price axis as a change in the economy's productive capacity

questions.explanation: Potential output is set by the quantity and quality of the factors of production and by the technology that combines them, so a bigger capital stock, a bigger workforce, or a more productive technique each move the vertical line to the right. The price level is the variable the long-run curve is drawn against, so a change in it is a movement along the line rather than a shift of it, and a purely monetary change in it changes the money value of output without changing the physical capacity to produce. This is the sense in which potential output is independent of the cycle and of the price level.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change alters the factors available or the technology using them.

questions.topic: Labour force growth and potential output
questions.learningObjective: compute the effect of labour force growth on potential output
questions.stem: Output in a labour-intensive economy follows Y = K^0.3 L^0.7, and with a capital stock of 1,000 and employment of 1,000 it produces 1,000 billion. Employment alone now rises by 5 percent with capital unchanged. What is the new level of output? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Employment enters with an exponent of 0.7, so the growth factor is 1.05 raised to 0.7, that is 1.034743, and output becomes 1,000 times 1.034743, or 1,034.74 billion. The constant-returns shortcut gives 0.7 times 5, that is 3.5 percent, and therefore 1,035 billion, which is within a rounding of the exact 1,034.7. The important point for a per person measure is that the labour weight is the larger one, so labour grows contribute more to aggregate potential output than equal percentage gains in capital do.
questions.hint: Weight the labour change by the exponent on labour, then apply it to the starting output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Total factor productivity and potential output
questions.learningObjective: compute the effect of a productivity change on potential output
questions.stem: Output in an economy follows Y = A K^0.3 L^0.7, and output is currently 1,000 billion. Total factor productivity then rises by 2 percent with both the capital stock and employment held fixed. By what percentage does output rise?

options.text: 2.0 percent, because productivity enters the production function with an exponent of one
1.4 percent, because the change is weighted by the exponent on labour, which is 0.7
options.misconception: weights a productivity change by an input's exponent instead of its own

options.text: 0.6 percent, because the change is weighted by the exponent on capital, which is 0.3
options.misconception: weights a productivity change by the capital exponent instead of its own

options.text: 20.0 percent, because a 2 percent rise in the factor multiplying output multiplies output by 20
options.misconception: reads the percentage change in the multiplier as if it were the change in output

questions.explanation: Productivity appears as A raised to the first power, so a 2 percent rise in A is passed through to output one for one, giving 1,000 times 1.02, or 1,020 billion. Substituting confirms it directly: 1.02 times 1,000^0.3 times 1,000^0.7 is 1.02 times 10^3, which is 1,020. The exponents 0.3 and 0.7 belong to the measured inputs, not to productivity, and adding them to 1 is what distinguishes a permanent growth gain from a one-off level gain, since only a permanent gain keeps feeding the long-run growth rate.
questions.hint: Check the exponent attached to productivity in the production function.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why long-run aggregate supply is vertical
questions.learningObjective: explain why potential output is independent of the price level
questions.stem: In the long run the classical model holds that output returns to potential whatever the price level does. What is the mechanism that fixes output there independently of prices?

options.text: Wages and prices are fully flexible, so any excess demand raises prices until real output is brought back to potential
Wages and prices are fixed by contract, so firms cannot cut prices to clear the market for their product
options.misconception: attributes a vertical long-run curve to price stickiness, which is a short-run idea

options.text: The central bank sets the price level directly, so output follows whatever level it chooses to install
options.misconception: assumes a direct administrative control over the price level

options.text: Technology determines output, so nothing about prices can influence how much is produced over any horizon
options.misconception: denies the price level any influence even in the short run

questions.explanation: Verticality at potential requires that the price level do no work in the adjustment. With flexible wages and prices, an output above potential bids up nominal wages, which raises costs, which reduces the real quantity of labour firms want, which brings output back; the mirror process runs when output is below potential. The mechanism is therefore a flexible price, not an administered one, and it is the same flexiblity that makes a permanent money expansion change only the price level. The short-run counterpart is the opposite assumption, sticky prices and sticky wages, which is what lets demand policy move output at all.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to nominal wages when output sits away from potential.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Short-run aggregate supply from sticky wages
questions.learningObjective: explain why the short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward
questions.stem: Why does the short-run aggregate supply curve slope upward when nominal wages are set in advance and adjust only slowly?

options.text: A higher price level cuts the real value of the fixed nominal wage, so firms gain from hiring more labour and output rises
A higher price level raises the nominal cost of every input, so firms pass it on in prices and profit per unit does not rise
options.misconception: ignores that a higher price level with a sticky nominal wage reduces the real cost of labour

options.text: A higher price level lowers the real value of the money stock, which forces firms to borrow at higher interest rates
options.misconception: attaches the short-run supply slope to the money market rather than to real wages

options.text: A higher price level raises real profits directly, so firms supply more at every price level with no cost involved
options.misconception: claims firms gain from output prices without any offsetting rise in costs

questions.explanation: Wages are set in money terms for a period, so when the price level rises the real cost of each unit of labour, W over P, falls while the real revenue per unit of output, P over P, is unchanged. The gap between the price received and the real wage paid is squeezed in the firm's favour, and profit per unit rises, so the firm hires more and produces more. That gap closes when workers revise their money wage expectations, which is exactly why the long-run curve is vertical and the short-run one is not.
questions.hint: Fix the nominal wage and ask what happens to the real wage when prices rise.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A money wage rise with fully flexible prices
questions.learningObjective: determine the effect of a money wage increase when prices adjust fully
questions.stem: A union secures a 5 percent increase in nominal wage rates across an economy, and prices in every other market are free to adjust without friction. What is the effect on the real wage, real output, and employment?

options.text: The real wage rises, real output falls, and employment falls, because the higher labour cost shifts the supply curve up
The real wage falls, real output rises, and employment rises, because a money wage gain raises demand for labour
options.misconception: reverses the ratio that defines the real wage and gets the sign of employment backwards

options.text: The real wage is unchanged, real output is unchanged, and employment is unchanged, because nominal wages alone are neutral
options.misconception: treats a change in money wages as automatically neutral in every sense

options.text: The real wage rises by 5 percent, real output rises, and employment rises, because money wages only ever expand output
options.misconception: assumes a higher money wage must raise real output and never contracts it

questions.explanation: The real wage is the money wage over the price level. If money wages rise by 5 percent and prices are free to move, the price level rises to keep the real wage from rising, so the real cost of labour does increase and firms hire less. Output and employment both fall and the short-run supply curve shifts up, which is the cost-push channel. A union wage settlement only fails to raise the real wage when it is matched by a matching rise in the general price level, and that is the sense in which a surprise money wage increase is inflationary.
questions.hint: Ask what prices must do to the real wage before the money wage increase can bite.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: An adverse supply shock in a linear model
questions.learningObjective: compute the new short-run equilibrium after a supply shock
questions.stem: An economy is described by the two curves aggregate demand P = 240 minus 0.6Y and short-run aggregate supply P = 60 plus 0.4Y, with the price level P and output Y in consistent units. A rise in the world price of oil raises production costs, which shifts the supply curve to P = 80 plus 0.4Y. What is the new short-run equilibrium level of real output?

options.text: 160, because setting 240 minus 0.6Y equal to 80 plus 0.4Y gives Y = 160
180, because a supply shock changes the price level but leaves the equilibrium output gap untouched
options.misconception: supposes the shock moves the curve without moving the equilibrium

options.text: 200, because the supply shock eventually restores output to the economy's potential level
options.misconception: reports the long-run potential level as if it were the short-run equilibrium

options.text: 140, because a rise in the supply intercept of 20 must cut equilibrium output by exactly 20
options.misconception: takes the intercept change as an equal and opposite change in output

questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires the two curves to agree, so 240 minus 0.6Y equals 80 plus 0.4Y, which gives 160 equals Y, and the price level is then 240 minus 96, that is 144, while the supply curve confirms it at 80 plus 64, also 144. Because the slopes have opposite signs, part of the intercept rise is absorbed by output and part by the price level, which is why the output loss, 20, is larger than either slope would suggest from the intercept alone. The price level rises at the same time as output falls, and that combination is what economists call stagflation.
questions.hint: Set the two expressions for the price level equal and solve for output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Stagflation from an adverse supply shock
questions.learningObjective: define stagflation and identify its source
questions.stem: A central bank describes an episode in which the unemployment rate rose while the inflation rate also rose. What is the name of that combination, and what is the usual first-order cause of it?

options.text: Stagflation, usually caused by an adverse supply shock that raises costs while the level of demand is unchanged
Reflation, usually caused by an expansionary demand policy that raises spending faster than prices adjust
options.misconception: names the opposite combination, in which output and prices rise together

options.text: Disinflation, usually caused by a monetary contraction that lowers inflation while output contracts
options.misconception: names the fall in the inflation rate, not a simultaneous rise in both series

options.text: A recession, usually caused by a fall in aggregate demand that lowers output but leaves prices unchanged
options.misconception: describes falling output with a stable price level and calls it stagflation

questions.explanation: Stagflation is the joint occurrence of rising unemployment and rising inflation, and an adverse supply shock produces it directly: costs rise, the supply curve shifts up, and the economy lands on it at lower output and a higher price level, which is lower output and therefore higher unemployment. An expansionary demand policy can also raise inflation, but it raises output with it, so unemployment falls rather than rises. The label matters for policy because a demand response to a supply-driven price rise only buys output at the cost of adding to the price level.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two series moved in the same direction or in opposite directions.

questions.topic: Full equilibrium response to a supply shock
questions.learningObjective: compute the price level and output following a supply shock
questions.stem: An economy has aggregate demand P = 240 minus 0.6Y and short-run aggregate supply P = 60 plus 0.4Y. First report the initial equilibrium price level, then the price level after a supply shock that moves the supply curve to P = 80 plus 0.4Y. Give both in the order asked.

132 then 132, because a pure cost shock changes real output but never the price level
options.misconception: holds the price level fixed when the supply intercept has risen

options.text: 144 then 132, because the initial equilibrium is the one after the shock in this ordering
options.misconception: swaps the two equilibria, treating the shocked state as the starting point

options.text: 132 then 152, because the price level is assumed to rise by the whole 20 unit shift of the supply intercept
options.misconception: adds the intercept shift to the old equilibrium price instead of solving the new intersection

After the shock 240 minus 0.6Y equals 80 plus 0.4Y, so Y is 160 and the price level is 240 minus 96, that is 144, confirmed at 80 plus 64. The second stage is the one that identifies the episode: output fell from 180 to 160 while the price level rose from 132 to 144.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Expected prices and the short-run supply curve
questions.learningObjective: explain how expected prices shift the short-run aggregate supply curve
questions.stem: Workers and firms form expectations about the future price level and set money wages and prices with reference to them. How does a rise in expected future inflation affect the short-run aggregate supply curve?

options.text: It shifts the curve up and left, because money wages are set from expected prices, so costs rise with expectations
It shifts the curve down and right, because higher expected inflation lowers the real value of today's money balances
options.misconception: confuses the demand-side real balance channel with the supply-side wage channel

options.text: It leaves the curve unchanged, because only realised input prices can move the cost structure of a firm
options.misconception: denies that the real cost of labour depends on prices workers expect

options.text: It rotates the curve so that it becomes steeper, because expectations change the slope rather than the level of costs
options.misconception: claims expectations change the responsiveness of supply rather than its position

questions.explanation: If workers expect a higher price level, they ask for higher money wages, and if firms expect one, they set higher prices. Since the real wage is the money wage over the price level, both sides indexing to expected rather than current prices raises costs at every current price level, which shifts short-run aggregate supply up. That expectation-augmented channel is what makes the curve shift when expectations change, as distinct from a movement along it when the current price level changes, and it is the reason disinflation requires credibility rather than only patience.
questions.hint: Ask what money wages do when workers expect the price level to be higher next year.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Long-run equilibrium after a permanent loss of capacity
questions.learningObjective: compute the long-run equilibrium after the long-run supply curve shifts
questions.stem: An economy has aggregate demand P = 240 minus 0.6Y and potential output of 200, with a supply curve consistent with that. A permanent loss of productive capacity shifts potential output to 160, and the supply curve shifts with it. First report the new output, then the new long-run price level, giving them in that order.

options.text: 160 then 144, because the new long-run point is where the demand curve meets the shifted long-run supply line
200 then 120, because potential output is unaffected by anything short of a change in the labour force
options.misconception: leaves potential output at its old value and ignores the capacity loss

options.text: 180 then 132, because the pre-shock intersection of the two curves survives the shift of long-run supply
options.misconception: reports the old equilibrium as if nothing had shifted

options.text: 160 then 120, because the price level at the old potential carries over to the new one unchanged
options.misconception: pairs the new output with the old long-run price level

questions.explanation: A permanent loss of capacity moves the vertical line to 160, so long-run output is 160 by definition, and the price level is read off aggregate demand there, giving 240 minus 0.6 times 160, that is 240 minus 96, or 144. Because the shock took potential itself down, the new short-run equilibrium and the new long-run equilibrium are the same point, and there is no output gap left for anyone to close. The economy ends up permanently poorer with a permanently higher price level, and no demand policy can undo either part of that.
questions.hint: Output is pinned by potential, so the price level must come from the demand curve.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Temporary against permanent supply shocks
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the policy consequences of temporary and permanent adverse supply shocks
questions.stem: A central bank must choose how hard to lean against a rise in the price of oil. How does the distinction between a temporary and a permanent cost increase change the available response?

options.text: A temporary increase reverses itself, so leaning against it risks locking in a needless contraction, while a permanent one leaves no output gap to close
A temporary increase leaves a permanent gap, so leaning against it is always the higher priority of the two
options.misconception: reverses which case leaves a gap that policy can close

options.text: The two cases are identical, because a cost increase is a cost increase once it is announced
options.misconception: ignores the fact that long-run potential differs between the two cases

options.text: A permanent increase returns output to potential by itself, so no policy response is ever needed in that case
options.misconception: claims a permanent supply problem is self-correcting at the original potential

questions.explanation: When the cost increase is temporary, wages and prices eventually come back down as expectations return to the old price path, and output returns to the original potential, so tightening into the shock buys a permanent output loss to avoid a temporary price rise. When the loss of capacity is permanent, potential itself is lower, the economy is at its new long-run equilibrium with no gap, and there is no output to recover by accepting a lower price level. The correct response also depends on whether the policy is credible, because an accommodating central bank can make a temporary shock permanent by validating it.
questions.hint: Ask whether potential output is different after the shock has run its course.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Self-correction of a recessionary gap
questions.learningObjective: compute the long-run outcome of a recessionary gap in a linear model
questions.stem: An economy has aggregate demand P = 240 minus 0.6Y, a short-run aggregate supply curve of P = 60 plus 0.4Y, and potential output of 200. It is in a recessionary gap with no policy action. What is the price level once the economy has returned to potential? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The initial intersection is at Y = 180 and a price level of 132, which is 20 below potential, so unemployment is above its natural rate and money wages fall. The lower wage cuts the supply intercept until the curve passes through the demand curve at potential, and there the price level is 240 minus 0.6 times 200, that is 120. The second route is the same statement: the supply curve that meets aggregate demand at 200 must have an intercept of 200 minus 0.4 times 200, that is 120, and it is the fall in wages, not anything on the demand side, that gets the economy there.
questions.hint: Put the long-run output at potential and read the price level off the demand curve.

questions.topic: Self-correction of an inflationary gap
questions.learningObjective: compute the long-run outcome of an inflationary gap in a linear model
questions.stem: Aggregate demand in an economy is P = 200 minus 0.6Y, its short-run aggregate supply curve is P = 40 plus 0.4Y, and potential output is 140. With no policy action, what are the long-run levels of real output and the price level?

options.text: 140 and 116, because wages rise until the supply curve meets demand at potential output
160 and 104, because the initial intersection of the two curves is already a long-run outcome
options.misconception: reads the short-run intersection as if it were the long-run equilibrium

options.text: 140 and 140, because the price level and the output level converge to the same number
options.misconception: assumes the price level ends up equal to the level of output

options.text: 160 and 116, because wages rise but the price level cannot rise before the supply curve moves
options.misconception: raises the price level without ever moving the supply curve

questions.explanation: The short-run intersection is 200 minus 0.6Y equal to 40 plus 0.4Y, so Y is 160 and the price level is 104, which is 20 above potential, so unemployment is below its natural rate and money wages rise. Wages rising shifts the supply curve up until the economy is back at potential, and at Y = 140 aggregate demand gives a price level of 200 minus 84, that is 116. The check that the long-run point lies on the demand curve is the same as saying the nominal value of output at potential is what the long-run price level delivers.
questions.hint: Find the short-run gap first, then impose the long-run condition on output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The mechanism of self-correction
questions.learningObjective: describe how an inflationary gap closes without any policy action
questions.stem: An economy is running above potential output and no government or central bank action is taken. Through what sequence does the gap close?

options.text: Unemployment below its natural rate bids wages up, which raises costs, shifts the supply curve up, and brings output back to potential
Unemployment below its natural rate bids wages down, which lowers costs, shifts the supply curve down, and brings output back
options.misconception: gets the direction of the wage pressure backwards for an economy above potential

options.text: Consumers anticipate the gap closing, so they save more, which lowers demand and returns output to potential
options.misconception: puts the adjustment in the saving behaviour of households rather than in the labour market

options.text: Firms expect higher wages, so they cut investment, which lowers demand and returns output to potential
options.misconception: attributes the adjustment to investment rather than to wages and costs

questions.explanation: The gap is defined by where output sits relative to potential, and potential is the level at which unemployment equals its natural rate, so output above potential means unemployment below it. Employers competing for scarce labour bid money wages up, and with the price level not yet fully adjusted the real cost of labour rises, which moves firms up their supply curve. As the supply curve moves up, output falls back toward potential and the price level rises, and the process stops when the labour market clears at the natural rate.
questions.hint: Locate the gap in the labour market, not in the goods market.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: What demand policy cannot change
questions.learningObjective: explain why demand-side policy cannot lower the natural rate of unemployment
questions.stem: A government doubles its spending for one year and real output rises by 12 percent, well above its starting level. What does the episode establish about the unemployment rate, and what does it leave untouched?

options.text: It shows unemployment fell below its natural rate for as long as the demand lasted, and it leaves the natural rate itself unchanged
It shows unemployment fell permanently below its natural rate, since the extra spending sustained the level of output
options.misconception: treats a temporary demand injection as a permanent change in labour market structure

options.text: It shows the natural rate fell, because more demand for labour draws discouraged workers back into the search process
options.misconception: credits a demand boost with a permanent change in the labour supply or matching structure

options.text: It shows unemployment could not have fallen at all, because the labour force does not respond to demand at any horizon
options.misconception: denies any short-run response of employment to aggregate demand

questions.explanation: The natural rate is the unemployment rate consistent with the labour market clearing at potential output, and it is set by frictions in matching workers to jobs, by the structure of unemployment benefits, by minimum wages, and by the efficiency of the search process. None of those responds to the level of spending, so a demand boost can push unemployment below the natural rate but cannot move the natural rate itself. When the spending is withdrawn, the supply curve has shifted as wages rise, and the economy returns to potential with a higher price level and the same natural rate.
questions.hint: Separate the level of unemployment from the rate that the labour market structure sets.

questions.topic: A demand expansion with sticky prices
questions.learningObjective: compute short-run output when prices are sticky after a demand shift
questions.stem: An economy has aggregate demand P = 240 minus 0.6Y and a short-run aggregate supply curve of P = 60 plus 0.4Y, giving an equilibrium of output 180 at a price level of 132. Prices are then sticky, and a monetary expansion shifts aggregate demand to P = 270 minus 0.6Y. What is the new level of real output? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: With the price level pinned at its old value of 132, the new demand curve gives 132 = 270 minus 0.6Y, so 0.6Y is 138 and Y is 230. The second route is to invert the demand equation for output, which is Y = 450 minus 1.667P, and substitute the fixed price level to get 450 minus 220, that is 230. The reason the answer is 230 rather than something smaller is that a sticky price removes the interest rate channel entirely for as long as it lasts, so the whole demand shift reaches output instead of being damped by a rising rate.
questions.hint: Hold the price level at its old value and solve the new demand curve for output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Sticky prices then flexible prices
questions.learningObjective: trace the price level from a sticky-price equilibrium to the long run
questions.stem: In the economy with aggregate demand initially P = 240 minus 0.6Y and supply P = 60 plus 0.4Y, a monetary expansion moves demand to P = 270 minus 0.6Y. First report the price level while prices are sticky, then the price level once the economy has returned to potential output of 200. Give the two in that order.

options.text: 132 then 150, because the price level is fixed first and then resets at the new long-run point
150 then 132, because the long-run price level is set before prices have any chance to move
options.misconception: reverses the order in which the two prices are determined

options.text: 132 then 240, because the intercept of the new demand curve becomes the long-run price level
options.misconception: treats a curve intercept as if it were a price level at an equilibrium

options.text: 150 then 150, because a monetary expansion raises prices at once when prices are sticky
options.misconception: denies any difference between the sticky and the flexible price level

questions.explanation: Sticky prices hold the price level at 132, and the economy moves along a horizontal supply line to output 230, which is 30 above potential. Once wages and prices adjust, the supply curve shifts up until output is back at 200, and the price level is then read off the new demand curve, which gives 270 minus 0.6 times 200, that is 150. The total rise of 18 is the whole price-level consequence of the expansion, of which none appears while prices are sticky and all of it appears afterwards.
questions.hint: The sticky price is the old one; the flexible price is the new curve read at potential.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why sticky prices make demand policy effective
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which sticky prices transmit demand policy to output
questions.stem: Why is a demand expansion able to raise real output in the short run rather than only the price level?

options.text: Because firms meet the extra demand by expanding output at prices they cannot yet raise to clear the market
Because sticky prices stop the interest rate from responding, so no spending is crowded out by a higher rate
options.misconception: attributes the whole effect to the interest rate and ignores the pricing decision

options.text: Because sticky prices make real money balances rise, which lowers real rates even when nominal rates are fixed
options.misconception: confuses the real balance channel with the price stickiness that blocks it

options.text: Because sticky prices reduce the size of the multiplier, so each unit of extra spending has a smaller but certain effect
options.misconception: misreads the direction of the multiplier under price stickiness

questions.explanation: Firms choose a price and a quantity, and when the price is set in advance the extra demand cannot push it up within the period, so the excess demand shows up as extra sales and firms respond by hiring and producing more. That is the entire short-run transmission: the price is a decision made before the demand is observed. A sticky price does also break the link from the price level to real balances, so interest rates do not rise and spending is not crowded out, which amplifies the effect, but the basic reason output moves is that the price cannot clear the market.
questions.hint: Ask what a firm does with excess demand when its price is already set.

questions.topic: Long-run effect of a pure demand expansion
questions.learningObjective: compute the long-run price level after an aggregate demand shift
questions.stem: An economy has aggregate demand P = 240 minus 0.6Y, potential output of 200, and a supply curve consistent with that potential. An increase in spending shifts aggregate demand to P = 270 minus 0.6Y. What is the price level once the economy has returned to potential output? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: In the long run output is potential, so the price level is the one the new demand curve gives at 200, that is 270 minus 0.6 times 200, or 150. The comparison that identifies the result is with the old long-run price level, which was 240 minus 120, that is 120, so the shift of 30 in the demand intercept shows up as a rise of 30 in the long-run price level once the two slopes have absorbed the change in output. Output ends where it started because nothing on the supply side has moved, which is the sense in which a pure demand change is a pure price-level change in the long run.
questions.hint: In the long run output is pinned by potential, so read the price level off the demand curve there.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Monetary neutrality in the long run
questions.learningObjective: state the long-run neutrality of money and the assumptions it rests on
questions.stem: Under what set of conditions does an increase in the money stock change the price level and nothing else?

options.text: When velocity is stable, all prices including wages are fully flexible, and output is at potential on both sides
When money demand is interest inelastic, because a stable money demand function keeps velocity fixed
options.misconception: gives a condition on money demand the role of the full flexiblity assumption

options.text: When the central bank holds the policy rate fixed, because a fixed rate prevents the money stock from affecting spending
options.misconception: treats the policy rate as the constraint that blocks monetary transmission

options.text: When the budget is balanced, because a balanced budget removes the government's demand for the new money
options.misconception: ties monetary neutrality to the fiscal position, which is not the condition

questions.explanation: Neutrality is a long-run statement resting on two things: the classical dichotomy, that real variables are determined by real conditions, and the quantity identity, that a sustained rise in the money stock shows up as a rise of the price level in proportion to the money growth once velocity is stable. The full flexiblity of wages and prices is what guarantees that output returns to potential, so no part of the increase is absorbed by higher real output. The short run breaks all of this at once, which is why the qualification long run carries so much weight.
questions.hint: Neutrality needs a classical dichotomy, a stable velocity, and a flexible price.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Short-run non-neutrality of money
questions.learningObjective: explain why money is not neutral over short horizons
questions.stem: In a model with sticky wages and sticky prices, what does a one-off increase in the money stock do to real output, and what does it do to the price level?

options.text: It raises real output, because sticky prices stop the interest rate from rising and spending rises instead
It leaves real output unchanged and raises the price level at once, because neutrality holds at every horizon
options.misconception: applies a long-run result at a short-run horizon

options.text: It raises real output and the price level together, because both respond identically to a change in nominal spending
options.misconception: claims a single money increase must be purely nominal as well as real

options.text: It lowers real output, because a larger nominal money stock must raise real interest rates and cut spending
options.misconception: reverses the sign of the real rate effect of a monetary expansion

questions.explanation: With the price level fixed for the period, an increase in the money stock raises real money balances, the interest rate falls, and planned spending rises with it, so firms meet the extra demand by producing more. Prices are sticky precisely because they were set before the extra money arrived, so none of the increase is absorbed by the price level on impact. As expectations catch up, wages and prices adjust, the supply curve moves up, and the remaining effect ends up entirely in the price level, which is the transition from short run to long run.
questions.hint: Fix the price level first, then ask where the extra money demand goes.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Long-run price effect of a money expansion
questions.learningObjective: compute the long-run price level implied by a money expansion
questions.stem: Output and velocity are unchanged, the price level starts at an index of 100, and the central bank raises the money stock by 20 percent on a one-off basis. What is the price level index once the economy has fully adjusted? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The quantity identity MV = PY with V and Y unchanged means that the price level moves in proportion to the money stock, so the index goes from 100 to 120. The cross-check is to watch the real balances: the money stock is 1.2 times its old value, so for real balances to return to their original level the price level must also be 1.2 times its old value, which is exactly 120. The path differs from the endpoint, since with sticky prices real balances rose first and output absorbed the change, but the fully adjusted price level is the same whatever the route.
questions.hint: Hold velocity and output fixed and let the price level absorb the whole change.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why the price level is the long-run variable
questions.learningObjective: explain why real money balances cannot stay above their original level
questions.stem: A central bank expands the money stock by 30 percent and real balances rise by 30 percent. Explain why that extra 30 percent of real money balances cannot persist once the economy has fully adjusted.

answer.exemplar: Real money balances are the nominal stock divided by the price level, and the only way for the ratio to stay above its original value is for the price level not to rise at all. But with sticky prices gone, the extra real balances lower the interest rate, which raises spending, which raises the price level; the ratio therefore falls back towards its starting value and the whole adjustment lands in the price level. Because money is neutral in the long run, the money stock ends up 30 percent larger with the price level 30 percent higher and output and interest rates back where they were, so the extra purchasing power is a transfer from holders of money to holders of goods rather than a lasting gain in spending power.

questions.explanation: The adjustment runs from real balances to the interest rate to spending to the price level, and each step reverses the previous one, so the only variable left to absorb a permanent change in the money stock is the price level. Once the price level has risen enough to bring the ratio of money to prices back down, the interest rate and spending are where they started and there is nothing left to correct. The persistent rise in real balances is what students should find puzzling, and the answer is that it is the temporary state, not the equilibrium one.
questions.hint: Ask which variable can absorb a permanent change in the money stock.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The multiplier in the spending model against the aggregate demand diagram
questions.learningObjective: reconcile the simple spending multiplier with the damped result in an aggregate demand diagram
questions.stem: In a simple spending model with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.75, a rise in government purchases of 40 billion is predicted to raise output by 160 billion. Drawn in an aggregate demand and aggregate supply diagram, the same policy appears to shift aggregate demand by 40 and to raise output by far less. Why?

options.text: The diagram includes the interest rate channel, so rising output bids up interest rates and crowds out private spending
The diagram uses a different marginal propensity to consume from the one the spending model was built on
options.misconception: invents a parameter difference that the question does not posit

options.text: The multiplier of 4 already accounts for the interest rate channel, so the diagram must be double counting it
options.misconception: claims the textbook multiplier includes a channel it deliberately omits

options.text: The diagram measures the change in the price level rather than the change in real output
options.misconception: confuses which variable the horizontal axis of the diagram carries

questions.explanation: The simple spending model holds the interest rate fixed by construction, so the only adjustment mechanism available to it is the one it built in, giving 1 over 1 minus 0.75, that is 4, and 40 times 4 is 160. The aggregate demand diagram adds the money market, so part of the extra spending is absorbed by a rise in interest rates that cuts private investment and interest-sensitive consumption, leaving less than 160 for total output. The two results are not rival estimates of the same thing, they are the same multiplier at two different degrees of monetary accommodation, which is exactly why estimates of the empirical multiplier depend on how the policy rule is specified.
questions.hint: Ask what the spending model leaves out that the diagram includes.

questions.topic: A devaluation as a demand shifter
questions.learningObjective: compute short-run output after a devaluation raises net exports
questions.stem: An economy has aggregate demand P = 240 minus 0.6Y, a supply curve P = 60 plus 0.4Y, and an equilibrium of output 180 at a price level of 132. questions.explanation: Holding the price level at 132, the new demand curve gives 132 = 258 minus 0.6Y, so 0.6Y is 126 and Y is 210. Output is 10 above potential rather than the 30 that a 30 unit demand shift would have produced, because net exports respond to the level of income, so part of any increase in spending is worked back as extra imports. The devaluation also raises the domestic price of imports, which shifts the supply curve up, so the short run and long run effects differ even though both curves move at once.
questions.hint: Fix the price level, then divide the distance from the new intercept by the demand slope.

questions.topic: A real appreciation as a demand shifter
questions.learningObjective: identify the effect of a real appreciation on aggregate demand
questions.stem: A country's real exchange rate appreciates by 10 percent because its productivity rises while its currency is fixed. What happens to its aggregate demand, and through what channel?

options.text: It shifts left, because domestic goods become relatively more expensive and net exports fall
It shifts right, because a stronger currency raises the domestic money value of foreign goods on offer
options.misconception: reads a rise in the price of imports as extra spending inside the country

options.text: It does not move, because aggregate demand is written in domestic currency and the currency does not change
options.misconception: supposes a real change in relative prices leaves net exports untouched

options.text: It shifts left, because a stronger currency lowers the domestic money value of domestic exports
options.misconception: uses the wrong direction for the effect on the currency value of exports

questions.explanation: The real exchange rate compares the domestic price level with the foreign price level converted at the going rate, so a 10 percent rise means domestic goods have become dearer relative to foreign ones. Foreign buyers take fewer domestic goods and domestic buyers take more foreign ones, so net exports fall and the spending schedule shifts down. A productivity-driven appreciation is the classic case, since higher productivity raises domestic prices and wages, and the loss of competitiveness is the demand-side cost of that gain.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the price comparison the currency change has moved.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The accelerator principle
questions.learningObjective: describe how the accelerator makes demand shocks larger
questions.stem: In the accelerator principle, planned investment responds to the change in output rather than to its level. What does that assumption imply for the size of a demand expansion?

options.text: The expansion is amplified, because higher output induces further investment, which induces still higher output
The expansion is damped, because investment responds to output and therefore subtracts from the initial increase
options.misconception: reads a reinforcing response as if it worked in the opposite direction

options.text: The expansion is unchanged, because investment is a function of output and so cannot alter the size of the change in output
options.misconception: assumes a behavioural response cannot feed back into the variable it responds to

options.text: The expansion lasts longer, because investment responds to the level of output and is therefore slow to reverse
options.misconception: confuses the accelerator with the persistence of a spending level

questions.explanation: If investment is written as a function of the change in output, then a rise in output calls forth new capital spending, and that spending is itself part of aggregate demand, so it calls forth a further rise in output. The amplification comes from the feedback loop, and the same reasoning runs the other way, because a fall in output releases no new investment demand and so makes the contraction larger than the spending that caused it. The price of the mechanism is instability, which is why the accelerator is used to explain the pace of the cycle rather than its direction.
questions.hint: Ask whether investment responds to the level of output or to the change in it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The financial accelerator
questions.learningObjective: explain how a credit shock amplifies a small change in spending
questions.stem: After a small fall in household spending, banks tighten their lending standards and planned investment then collapses by far more than the original fall. Describe the mechanism that turns a modest shock into a large one.

answer.exemplar: The mechanism runs through the balance sheet of a firm that finances capital with bank credit. A small fall in spending lowers sales and cash flow, which raises the probability that the firm cannot repay, so its external finance premium rises and its credit is rationed. Higher borrowing costs then cut investment, which lowers demand again and worsens the cash flow of every other borrower, so the original shock is magnified and can persist. The loop is strongest where collateral values move with the cycle, since a fall in land or equity prices shrinks the collateral backing the loans and worsens the same balance sheets. This is why a credit channel is treated as a distinct source of amplification rather than a synonym for the interest rate channel, and why the collapse of a credit channel is far more dangerous than the original shock.

questions.explanation: The external finance premium is the spread between the cost of bank credit and the cost of issuing claims, and it depends on the borrower's balance sheet rather than on the general interest rate. A small shock moves it, and because it multiplies through investment, it turns a modest change in spending into a much larger one. The loop also has a limit, since a sufficiently large shock makes credit unavailable altogether, which is why the effect is asymmetric and why recoveries are slow once the balance sheets have been damaged.
questions.hint: Ask what a firm's borrowing cost depends on besides the general interest rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The wealth effect on spending
questions.learningObjective: explain how a change in asset prices shifts aggregate demand
questions.stem: Households cut back on spending after house and equity prices fall, even though their money income has stopped falling. Explain why the wealth effect makes that response so large and so persistent.

answer.exemplar: Households hold wealth in the form of houses, equities and pension rights, and a large part of that wealth is never spent, so the marginal propensity to consume out of asset wealth is well below one. When asset prices rise the stock of net wealth rises, and households raise consumption by that marginal propensity times the gain, which is a component of the shift in aggregate demand. A fall in asset prices does the reverse, and because the effect runs through a stock of wealth it is unusually persistent, since a price that has fallen once has already destroyed a part of the balance sheet that has to be rebuilt before spending recovers. The channel also explains why consumer spending can fall in a recession even after real disposable income has stopped falling.

questions.explanation: Wealth differs from income in two ways that matter for spending. It is a stock, so a change in its price scales the whole balance rather than adding a flow, and households do not treat all of it as spendable, so only a fraction is converted into consumption. Those two features make the wealth effect larger than the effect of the same change in annual income, and they make it slower to reverse, since restoring a destroyed balance sheet takes time out of current consumption.
questions.hint: Separate the marginal propensity to consume out of wealth from the one out of income.

questions.learningObjective: identify a non-mechanical shifter of aggregate demand
questions.stem: Businesses postpone new orders while their owners expect the next quarter to be worse, and household spending falls on the same expectation. How do economists classify that change in spending?

A movement along aggregate demand, since the price level is unchanged while spending varies
options.misconception: calls a change in the spending schedule a movement along the resulting curve

options.text: A shift of short-run aggregate supply, since expectations are a cost rather than a spending determinant
options.misconception: moves the effect to the supply side, where expectations enter through costs

options.text: A change in potential output, since expectations about the future alter the labour an economy will employ

The same expectations also act on the supply side, since firms set prices and wages with reference to what they expect, so one piece of news can shift both curves and leave the direction of output genuinely uncertain.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A supply-side tax change
questions.learningObjective: explain why a well-designed supply-side tax change shifts both aggregate demand and long-run aggregate supply
questions.stem: A government cuts payroll taxes on newly hired workers while leaving everything else unchanged. Which of the two curves in the standard model does this policy unambiguously move, and why?

options.text: It moves long-run aggregate supply right, because it lowers the cost of hiring and so raises the labour employed at any real wage
It moves aggregate demand right by the whole tax cut, because a tax cut is an increase in disposable income
options.misconception: treats a supply-side tax change as if it were a pure transfer to spending

options.text: It moves short-run aggregate supply right, because a lower tax bill reduces firms' costs at the current price level
options.misconception: assigns a change in hiring costs to the price-setting side of the model

options.text: It moves neither curve, because the money value of a tax cut affects only nominal rather than real variables
options.misconception: denies that a change in a real cost can alter real behaviour

questions.explanation: A payroll tax cut on new hiring changes the price of labour, which is a determinant of how much labour firms want at any given real wage, so it belongs on the long-run supply side and moves the vertical line to the right. A tax cut on all income would also raise disposable income and shift demand, and a tax cut on profits would raise investment and shift demand, so the two channels are separable in principle and the design of the change decides which dominates. questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The sticky wage identification problem
questions.learningObjective: explain the empirical difficulty in distinguishing sticky wages from real shocks
questions.stem: Researchers observe that money wages barely fall in recessions and conclude that wages are sticky. Explain why that observation alone is weaker evidence for wage stickiness than it appears.

answer.exemplar: The observation is consistent with at least two distinct stories. Under the first, money wages are genuinely rigid, so firms absorb a fall in demand by cutting output rather than wages. Under the second, wages are fully flexible but the real wage is unchanged, which happens when a fall in the price level offsets any fall in the money wage, so firms see no change in their labour costs and again cut output. Separating the two requires watching the real wage, not the money wage, and even that is hard because the relevant price is the one firms face, which is not the one a consumer index records. The residual explanation, that workers are slow to renegotiate, and the measurement problem, that the deflator is wrong, are also observationally similar here.

questions.explanation: The difficulty is that a flat money wage is a statement about a nominal variable, while the decision firms make turns on the real one, so any evidence that holds the money wage fixed must be checked against the price level before it can be read as evidence of rigidity. On top of that, the relevant price for a firm's wage decision is the price of the output it sells, which need not be the price in any published index. Empirical work therefore leans on firm-level panel data or on policy-driven variation in expected inflation, where the two explanations make different predictions, and the answer to the question depends on which of those routes is used.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money wage or the real wage is the variable the theory predicts.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The sticky price identification problem
questions.learningObjective: explain the difficulty of separating sticky prices from real shocks in the data
questions.stem: A study finds that a monetary contraction lowers the price level only slowly and lowers output quickly. Why is that observation not a clean test of whether prices are sticky?

answer.exemplar: The pattern is the one the model predicts, but the same pattern is produced by a model with no price stickiness at all if the adjustment comes from the supply side. In a competitive model a monetary contraction reduces output because real balances fall, and the price level falls only to the extent needed to bring spending back to its starting level, which is a gradual process driven by the slow adjustment of wages and expectations rather than by any nominal rigidity. Telling the two apart requires more than the timing of the two series, because both models are slow on prices and fast on output. What would separate them is a prediction about a dimension the two models disagree on, such as whether the effect of a monetary shock depends on the real rate of interest or on the level of the price level, or on how the effect varies with the state of the economy.

questions.explanation: A test is only as strong as the alternative hypotheses it rules out, and the standard alternative here is a model in which every price clears every period and the gradualism comes from the labour side of the economy. Confirming the evidence would mean finding a prediction on which the two models disagree and testing it, which is why the research literature has leaned on state-dependent effects and on the response of the real rate rather than on the speed of the price level itself. The bare observation that prices are slow is consistent with both and settles neither.

The alternative is discretion, in which the authority sets the money wage directly and households revise the real wage they expect, which is precisely what pushes the actual unemployment rate below the natural rate.

The numerical value of the central bank's inflation target, which has no bearing on how wages are set

questions.topic: Why the size of the multiplier is contested
questions.learningObjective: explain the identification problem behind estimates of the output multiplier
questions.stem: Estimates of how much output responds to a fiscal injection vary widely, and the ones that use a research design driven by a policy rule rather than by an economic shock tend to be smaller. Explain the mechanism behind that difference.

answer.exemplar: An estimated multiplier is really an estimate of how much of a spending change reaches output, and that depends on how the spending was financed and offset. When the policy rule is one that responds to the state of the economy, a fiscal injection goes together with a monetary reaction and with private spending that is already moving, and a simple correlation attributes all of that movement to the injection, which inflates the estimate. A design driven by a political or formulaic rule that is uncorrelated with the business cycle avoids that, and the smaller estimate is the one that isolates the fiscal effect itself. The estimates are therefore not necessarily in conflict, since they answer different questions, and the honest statement of the result is a range whose value depends on the assumptions behind the design rather than a single number.

questions.explanation: The question is not only what the multiplier is but what the identifying assumption buys, and a multiplier estimated from a rule-driven instrument and a multiplier estimated from a discretionary response to a downturn answer different counterfactuals. The second includes the monetary offset that any modern central bank would supply, so it overstates the fiscal effect on its own. This is a general feature of applied macro rather than a peculiarity of the fiscal case, and it is why a policy recommendation that leans on a large multiplier needs to state the financing and monetary assumptions that make it true.
